title: Commits, Diff & History Inspection
description: Record immutable snapshots with git commit, compare changes with git diff, and navigate history using git log and git show.

blocks.content: A commit is a permanent snapshot of your project at a specific point in time. Each commit has a unique ID (a long string called a SHA), a message you write to describe what changed, and a timestamp with your name attached.

## Making a Commit

After staging your changes, save them with:
```
git commit -m "your message here"
```

A good commit message is short and describes **what changed and why**, not how:
- `add login button to navbar` - good
- `fix` - too vague
- `changed stuff` - useless

## Viewing History

See all past commits:
```
git log
```

A compact one-line view:
```
git log --oneline
```

Example output:
```
a3f9c12 fix broken image link on homepage
7b2d441 add contact form
e1a8009 initial commit
```

Each line is one commit. The short code on the left is the beginning of the commit's unique ID.

## Looking at a Specific Commit

See exactly what changed in a commit:
```
git show a3f9c12
```

Compare the current state to the last commit:
```
git diff
```

blocks.question: What does a commit save?
options: Only the files you currently have open
A snapshot of everything in the staging area at that moment
The entire working directory including unstaged files
A backup of your local hard drive
blocks.explanation: A commit saves exactly what was in the staging area when you ran `git commit`. Files that were changed but not staged are not included. This is why the staging area is so important - it lets you be precise about what each commit contains.

blocks.prompt: Commit the staged changes with the message "initial commit".
